intro: The finale of Haydn’s Symphony No. 94, the “Surprise”, marked Allegro molto, opens with a quiet tune in the strings. Later the tune makes a false return, there is an outburst in the minor key, and a timpani roll comes in ahead of the orchestra.

sections.label: A · String theme, then added players
sections.mNote: Flute and bassoon join before the orchestra enters.

sections.label: Dev · Opening theme in G major
sections.mNote: The opening theme returns, then modulates to minor keys.

sections.label: A′ · Shorter return in G major
sections.mNote: The first tune returns without its repeated opening phrases.

sections.label: Coda · Timpani, then a turn to E♭
sections.mNote: The timpani crescendo before the rest of the orchestra.

cues.title: Opening theme and repeats
cues.text: The strings play the opening theme alone, and a flute joins them for the repeat. When the theme returns, flute and bassoon join the strings. The full orchestra enters after these statements, which take up bars 1–38.
cues.evidence: Finale, bars 1–38: strings, flute on the repeat, then flute and bassoon at the return. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second theme over a pedal D
cues.text: The second theme, from bar 75, is also quiet, and the strings again lead. Beneath it the bass repeats D for most of the theme while the harmony alternates between D major and A major.
cues.evidence: Finale, second theme from bar 75: string scoring and repeated D beneath alternating tonic and dominant harmonies. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Opening of the development
cues.text: The development opens with the first theme in G major, now with bassoon (bars 99–124). Its closing figure then moves into the bass and passes through a rapid succession of keys.
cues.evidence: Finale, opening of development, bars 99–124: return of the G major theme with bassoon, followed by its closing figure in the bass. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recapitulation and coda
cues.text: The recapitulation in G major begins at bar 182. It leaves out the repeated opening of the first theme and starts with its contrasting phrase, and Haydn cuts the transition between the two themes. The second theme returns in the home key, and the coda begins at bar 222.
cues.evidence: Finale, recapitulation from bar 182 and coda from bar 222. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, timpani roll and E♭ major
cues.text: The coda begins softly at bar 222 with the upbeat of the theme. A timpani roll reaches forte one bar before the rest of the orchestra, and the first theme returns in E♭ major.
cues.evidence: Finale, coda from bar 222: quiet opening, timpani roll with an early forte and E♭ major return of the first theme. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Return of the opening tune in G
transitions.from: A · String theme, then added players
transitions.to: Dev · Opening theme in G major
transitions.how: The exposition ends with three loud D chords. Repeated C notes then turn the harmony towards G major, and the opening tune returns with bassoon added to the strings. The tune’s closing figure then moves into the bass.
transitions.evidence: Finale, bars 99–112: exposition close, repeated C notes, G major theme and subsequent bass figure. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: Through D major to a shortened return
transitions.from: Dev · Opening theme in G major
transitions.to: A′ · Shorter return in G major
transitions.how: The development moves through E♭, F and B♭ major and then reaches D major. The first violins’ semiquavers come to a stop before G major returns. Haydn begins the recapitulation with the contrasting phrase of the first tune and cuts its repeated opening.
transitions.evidence: Finale, approach to the recapitulation and return from bar 182. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: Into the coda: timpani roll, E♭ major
transitions.from: A′ · Shorter return in G major
transitions.to: Coda · Timpani, then a turn to E♭
transitions.how: The second tune, in G major, leads straight into a quiet coda (bars 222–268) built on the opening upbeat. A timpani roll grows loud before the orchestra enters, and the harmony turns to E♭ major. The first tune returns forte in that key, and the movement closes on chords in G major.
transitions.evidence: Finale, coda, bars 222–268: timpani roll, E♭ major detour and closing chords. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

source.title: Haydn, Symphony No. 94, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, ed. Rietz, plate 8876, [1855])
source.locator: Finale, printed pp. 35–52: string opening, wind additions, full orchestra and the coda’s timpani roll.

timeline.note: The strings introduce the tune quietly on their own.
Flute joins the tune’s repeat; flute and bassoon join its next return.
The full orchestra enters forte while the violins continue their running figure.
In the coda the timpani play a roll that grows loud a bar before the orchestra.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition and any editorial alterations are not identified in the recording sources.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Young lists CVE-48988 with the recording date 24 April 1929, DAHR lists it among the Boston Symphony Orchestra and Koussevitzky recordings of Symphony No. 94 made that day, and the Bolig discography assigns the finale (“Allegro di molto”) to that matrix. Commons’ 1 January 1929 is not a session day.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
fields.note: Young heads the 22 April 1929 session “Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts” and lists the 24 April retaken sides of the same symphony under that session; DAHR gives Symphony Hall, Boston for the Andante side CVE-48984. A separate place for the 24 April retakes is not given.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Young lists the symphony as released 9/29 on M-55 (7058/60), with later AM-55, DM-55, HMV and LP issues. The upstream transfer also names set M-55 (Internet Archive description), and DAHR places the Andante on disc 7059. The disc number of this movement’s sides is not stated; the side order (sides 1–2 movement I, sides 3–4 the Andante, sides 5–6 the Menuetto and Finale) suggests 7058 for movement I and 7060 for the Menuetto and Finale, but that allocation is inferred.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: CVE-48988, take 2 or take 3: the finale; the take on this transfer is not identified
fields.note: Young lists both take 2 and take 3 of CVE-48988 as issued (three takes made), and Bolig names take 3. Which take the Bob Varney transfer reproduces is not established by any source consulted, so only the matrix is asserted. The DAHR matrix page could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Bob Varney — transfer from original Victor 78s

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was uploaded in December 2008, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Transfer from the original Victor 78 rpm set M-55 into one 20:48 file, from which the four movements were extracted as separate Commons files.
fields.note: The file lengths of the four Commons movements sum to the length of the Internet Archive file within about a second. The extraction procedure, stylus, playback curve, side-join locations and noise treatment are not documented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Haydn died in 1809. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the Koussevitzky/Boston recording attributed to 1929, and the Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons public-domain licence URL, not treated here as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The programme’s pre-1963 European rule applies because the 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension; Young gives the release as September 1929, which supports first publication well before 1963. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US status is not established.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he wrote in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three. He was a wheelwright’s son and had spent most of his adult life in the livery of a servant of the Esterházy family.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. As a chorister he sang church music daily but received little instruction in composition. Performances outside the cathedral also gave him chances to get a meal. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
